Summary and Source: Argentina signed a U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment (ARTI), with the labor commitment finalized around Feb 5, 2026: Argentina committed to "adopt and implement a prohibition on the importation of goods produced by forced or compulsory labor," placing it in USTR's lower 10% tariff tier. No domestic Argentine bill or implementing regulation has been found tabled yet -- this is a treaty-level commitment only, structurally the same situation as Jordan's Article 2.9 commitment, and is reclassified from "No" to "Partial" for consistency with that precedent. No Argentina-specific hearing testimony found in the July 7-9 hearing record. Source: USTR fact sheet, Nov 2025/Feb 2026; White & Case / Gibson Dunn (law firm summaries of USTR determination). A regime of post-market detection, sanctions and withdrawal is NOT a prohibition on importation, so even publication in the Boletin Oficial would NOT automatically move this row to Yes -- the text would have to be read first. (U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment: Argentina commits to adopt and implement a forced-labor import prohibition; treaty-level commitment only, no domestic bill/regulation tabled yet -- reclassified from No to Partial for consistency with Jordan's equivalent RTA-commitment-only precedent. OCTOBER 4, 2026 -- ARGENTINA IS A SIGNATORY TO THE G20 MILWAUKEE STATEMENT OF 2 OCTOBER 2026 -- the run's one genuinely new cross-cutting development, read here in full from the primary PDF on ustr.gov (2 pages, 3,657 characters). Its signatories are EXACTLY THREE: "We, the Trade Ministers of the United States, Argentina, and Mexico". Its operative passage is: "we recognize our opportunity and responsibility to work together to eliminate goods produced with forced labor from supply chains and international trade, including by adopting or maintaining and effectively enforcing measures that prohibit the importation or sale of goods produced wholly or in part with forced labor", together with "We support the exchange of information on traded goods produced with forced labor and best practices... including forced labor import prohibitions or market bans." IT CREATES NO NEW OBLIGATION AND CHANGES NO CLASSIFICATION, and the reasons are textual rather than assumed: it is a ministerial STATEMENT, not a treaty; its verbs are hortatory ("We call on all countries", "We encourage World Trade Organization Members"); and the key phrase is "adopting OR MAINTAINING", which is satisfied by what a signatory already has. It is therefore NOT an RTA commitment and does not add anyone to that watchlist. It usefully corroborates this tracker's own framing, noting that "Numerous economies have adopted, or committed to adopt, measures intended to stop the importation or placement on their market of products produced with forced labor". THE NOTABLE FACT IS THE NON-SIGNATURE OF THE OTHER SEVENTEEN G20 MEMBERS. For THIS row specifically: Argentina signing a statement that endorses import prohibitions does NOT convert its RTA commitment into a domestic instrument, so it stays Partial -- but it is a meaningful signal of intent from one of only three signatories, and it is the first positive Argentine action recorded on this row in months. Separately, a Spanish search again returned only Dominican items and unrelated Argentine customs decrees (e.g. Decreto 604/2026 on postal imports); no Argentine forced-labour decree was found, and the long-open question of whether Argentina's draft is an import prohibition at all (it is ex post by design) is STILL unsettled. OCTOBER 5, 2026 -- THE TREATY OBLIGATION IS NOW READ FROM THE PRIMARY TEXT, AND THE US HAS PUBLICLY DEMANDED COMPLIANCE THREE DAYS AFTER ARGENTINA SIGNED THE G20 STATEMENT. The US-Argentina ARTI PDF was read directly on ustr.gov. Article 2.9 ("Labor") paragraph 1: "Argentina shall adopt and effectively implement a prohibition on the importation of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part by forced or compulsory labor as defined by the relevant International Labor Organization (ILO) instruments to which it is a party. Argentina shall consider U.S. government determinations on entities under Section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930..." So Argentina's RTA commitment is verbatim-confirmed, as Indonesia's and Jordan's already were. THE NEW DEVELOPMENT: El Esquiu of 3 October reports Greer demanding Argentina comply with "un compromiso central pendiente" under "el articulo 2.9", and that Argentina lacks "un marco aduanero especifico en fronteras" -- the US publicly pressing a CO-SIGNATORY of the Milwaukee statement to actually legislate, which is a pointed juxtaposition. El Intransigente is reported to say no decree, draft or mechanism has been established. BOTH ARE SECONDARY and were read only in part, and they sit in mild tension with El Cronista's earlier "borrador" report, so they do not move the classification. But they sharpen what to watch: if Argentina answers with an actual customs instrument this row goes to Yes. The ex post question remains unsettled and no new Argentine text was found)

Summary and Source: The Customs Management (Amendment) Bill 2026 passed the House of Assembly alongside the 2026-2027 Budget, and the Bahamas government's own legislation portal lists it by name under "Tabled in House of Assembly." The block is now the longest run seen (it previously cleared after two days). Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (enacted: Customs Management (Amendment) Act, 2026, s.208A, in force 1 July 2026) -- RECLASSIFIED Partial -> Yes ON 6 OCTOBER 2026, AND THIS ROW HEREBY REVERSES ITS OWN RULING OF 22 SEPTEMBER. THE TEXT, READ HERE DIRECTLY FROM THE GOVERNMENT PDF: the Extraordinary Official Gazette of 1 July 2026 carries "CUSTOMS MANAGEMENT (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2026 ... AN ACT TO AMEND THE CUSTOMS MANAGEMENT ACT ... Enacted by the Parliament of The Bahamas", whose section 2 inserts a new section 208A reading: "208A. Prohibition on goods resulting from forced labour. The Minister may, by Order, prohibit the importation of any goods, wholly or partially produced or manufactured, from any supplier, country or territory if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the goods are a result of forced labour." Section 1(2): "This Act shall come into force on the 1st day of July, 2026." So it is enacted, gazette-published and IN FORCE. HOW THIS FILE GOT IT WRONG, because the failure is instructive. On 22 September this row FOUND Act 2026-0020 in the Acts register and EXCLUDED it on three grounds, the load-bearing one being that it "sits in an unbroken fiscal sequence" of appropriation, tariff, stamp, VAT and business-licence Acts and was therefore "the annual revenue package, not an import prohibition". THAT WAS AN INFERENCE FROM POSITION IN A LIST, and it was allowed to outweigh an unread text. The row even recorded at the time that the Act PDF "could NOT be read" -- "three image operators and only 65 words of recoverable text ... the operative text is a SCANNED IMAGE" -- and then honourably noted that "the burden sits with the positive claim". THE PDF IS NOT A SCAN. Fetched today with a cookie jar (seven HTTP 202 sgcaptcha refusals, then HTTP 200 on the EIGHTH attempt, application/pdf, 399,664 bytes, 3 pages), it extracts cleanly to a full text layer. The earlier "scanned image" conclusion was a failed extraction mistaken for a property of the document, and it should have been retested rather than carried for a fortnight. TWO FURTHER CONSEQUENCES. (i) THE TRIBUNE WAS RIGHT AND THIS FILE WAS WRONG TO REJECT IT: the 24 and 27 July lines describing "recently-passed reforms to the Customs Management Act that ban the importation of goods made with forced labour", "passed alongside the 2026-2027 Budget prior to end-June 2026", were declined here twice as the revenue-package conflation. They were accurate reporting. (ii) THE BILL/ACT DISTINCTION THIS ROW POLICED FOR WEEKS WAS A DISTINCTION WITHOUT A DIFFERENCE: the Bill (2026-0019) and the Act carry IDENTICAL s.208A text and the same First Schedule whisky/brandy amendment in s.3 -- the Bill simply became the Act, and the Bill's Objects and Reasons say it prohibits "goods from suppliers, places or countries that produce Force (Child) Labour - from entering the Bahamas". WHY "Yes" IS THE CONSISTENT CALL: s.208A is a DESIGNATION-DEPENDENT FRAMEWORK power ("The Minister may, by Order") and NO Order has been located, so nothing is yet prohibited in practice. But this file already classifies Trinidad and Tobago as Yes on Customs Act s.45(1)(w) ("as designated by the Minister", no designation list found) and India as Yes on FTP Para 2.20B (no designated goods ever found). The Bahamian provision is the same architecture, so consistency requires Yes; classifying it Partial would mean treating identical instruments differently. ONE ITEM LEFT UNRESOLVED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: in the extracted text the line "No. 20 of 2026 [Date of Assent - 30th June, 2026]" falls after "Page - 2" and immediately before the VALUE ADDED TAX (AMENDMENT) (NO. 2) ACT heading, so WHICH Act that assent line belongs to is ambiguous in reading order -- the same adjacency trap this row identified in reverse on 22 September. It does not matter for the classification, which rests on the Act's own "Enacted by the Parliament" and in-force clause plus gazette publication, but the assent date is recorded as unconfirmed. THE OPEN ITEM IS NOW THE MINISTERIAL ORDER: until one is made, s.208A prohibits nothing in practice, and finding or excluding such an Order is this row's next task.

After six days in which mincom.gov.bd was blocked site-side across every route, the Import Policy Order 2026-2029 was located as a PDF mirrored by a Bangladeshi law firm and downloaded here (HTTP 200, 723,681 bytes, application/pdf, 88 pages, verified genuine and not a shell). THE GAP HAS THEREFORE MOVED FROM ACCESS TO ENCODING, which is progress of a kind but changes nothing about what is known. The document's fonts are SutonnyMJ, Nikosh and Vrinda -- LEGACY NON-UNICODE BENGALI FACES that map bytes to glyphs with no ToUnicode table -- so extraction yields 302,960 characters of mojibake. A cmap-based decode was attempted and recovered NOTHING, because the nine ToUnicode blocks in the file belong to other fonts. The diagnosis is conclusive: of the 141 recognisable four-letter ASCII runs in the entire extraction, the most common are "name", "post", "prep", "hhea", "hmtx", "loca" and "cmap" -- these are PDF FONT-TABLE INTERNALS, not document text. NOT ONE READABLE ENGLISH SENTENCE EXISTS IN THE FILE. CONSEQUENTLY THE ZERO HITS FOR "forced", "labour", "compulsory", "convict" and "prison" ARE MEANINGLESS AND MUST NOT BE READ AS A NEGATIVE. What is needed now is either OCR, which this environment does not have, or a source reproducing the text in genuine Unicode Bengali or English -- a CCIE circular reproducing Appendix 1(b) in plain text remains the best lead, and other Bangladesh Gazette PDFs are likely to share the same legacy-font problem. The law-firm blog post that hosts the unreadable PDF was itself read, and its own text states that no information is mentioned regarding forced labour, convict labour or related prohibited imports -- BUT THAT IS THE BLOG DESCRIBING ITS OWN ARTICLE, NOT THE ORDER, and it is explicitly not adopted as evidence about the order's contents. The primary text is unread on its EIGHTH day, and this is a "not yet found" rather than a settled absence. Two extraction methods on one document disagreed completely, and the weaker one would have produced a false negative that left this row misclassified -- pypdfium2 is available in this environment and should be tried whenever the stream method returns an implausibly low word count. THE CLASSIFICATION IS PARTIAL, NOT YES, and the caveat is real: this is an unsponsored deputy's mocion with no votes recorded, drafted loosely around a presumption standard, and it may never advance. Under the standing rule a formally tabled bill is enough for Partial, and this one is formally tabled and expressly names importation. DECRETO 1444 DEL 28 DE SEPTIEMBRE DE 2026 HAS BEEN ISSUED, "por el cual se prohibe la importacion de bienes producidos total o parcialmente mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio, y se dictan otras disposiciones". VERIFIED TWICE AT PRIMARY SOURCE: the title, number and date were read on the Ministry of Commerce's own decree register at mincit.gov.co/normatividad/decretos/2026, whose "Ultima actualizacion" line now reads 28 de septiembre de 2026 -- the register had ceilinged at Decreto 1418 for eleven days; and the decree PDF itself was then downloaded (HTTP 200, 2,191,640 bytes) and text-extracted here, yielding 3,038 words with 31 occurrences of "forzoso", 21 of "prohib", 17 of "importaci" and 21 of "aduaner". THE OPERATIVE TEXT: Article 1, "Prohibicion de importacion de bienes producidos mediante trabajo forzoso", bars entry into the national customs territory of goods "que hayan sido, total o parcialmente, extraidas, producidas, manufacturadas o transformadas mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio", and extends to every stage of the supply chain including extraction, cultivation, harvest, manufacture, assembly and processing. Article 2 defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29. Article 18 provides that "El presente decreto rige a partir del dia siguiente de su publicacion en el Diario Oficial", under the exception in paragraph 2 of article 2 of Ley 1609 de 2013. WHY THIS IS "YES" AND NOT "PARTIAL": the standing policy reserves Yes for an ACTUALLY ENACTED instrument even if not yet fully effective, and this is a signed, numbered, dated decree on the issuing ministry's own register -- no longer the "Proyecto de Decreto" this row has tracked since the comment window closed on 15 August, forty-four days ago. ONE THING IS NOT VERIFIED AND IS FLAGGED: publication in the Diario Oficial itself was not confirmed, and since Article 18 keys entry into force to that publication, the decree may be enacted but not yet in force. Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (limb (c), an enacted but incomplete regime) -- RECLASSIFIED FROM No ON 1 OCTOBER 2026 ONCE THE TEXT WAS FINALLY READ; this row had been flagged the previous run as the most likely next change in the file and held at No only because the text was unread. The instrument is DECRETO EJECUTIVO N. 45941-H-MTSS-COMEX, signed 7 September 2026 and published in LA GACETA ON 28 SEPTEMBER, Alcance N. 129. Every account agrees it creates an official list of goods at risk of forced labour, with COMEX and MTSS to issue parameters within 60 calendar days and Hacienda supporting on customs. THE ACCOUNTS CONFLICT ON THE ONE POINT THAT DECIDES THE CLASSIFICATION: La Nacion says it "establishes a registry rather than imposing import prohibitions", with listing triggering "medidas de seguimiento y control" rather than automatic exclusion; El Observador states the aim is to "prohibit and prevent the entry" of such goods. Those cannot both be right about its legal effect, and no pass has read the decree. THE POSSIBLE OUTCOMES ARE ALL LIVE: if it is a registry with monitoring it is arguably a partial regime falling short of a prohibition, which is Partial under limb (c); if it actually prohibits entry it is an enacted instrument and Yes. Holding at No was the conservative reading and was explicitly PROVISIONAL pending the text. ON OCTOBER 1, 2026 THE TEXT WAS READ AND THE ROW MOVES No -> Partial. La Gaceta Alcance N.o 129 of 28 September 2026 was retrieved directly from the Imprenta Nacional (HTTP 200, 6.2 MB, 244 pages extracted with pypdfium2; pgrweb.go.cr returned 403) and the decree was read in full, independently by a research pass and then again at article level here. THE CONFLICT BETWEEN EL OBSERVADOR AND LA NACION IS RESOLVED IN LA NACION'S FAVOUR, and it turns on the difference between a purpose clause and an operative one. Article 1 (Objeto) does state the aim of "fundamentar medidas preventivas, de seguimiento y control ... para evitar que bienes que hayan sido producidos, extraidos o manufacturados, total o parcialmente, en cualquier pais o territorio aduanero, mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio, e incluso trabajo forzoso infantil, ingresen al territorio nacional" -- which read alone sounds like a ban, and is evidently what El Observador read. But the ONLY operative border provision, Article 12 (Medidas de Seguimiento y Control), says that when a listed good "se pretende ingresar al territorio nacional la autoridad competente adoptara las medidas de seguimiento y control correspondientes, de conformidad con el ordenamiento juridico" -- monitoring and control, NOT refusal of entry. Article 4 does contain a prohibition, but of forced labour "en el territorio nacional", i.e. domestic conduct, not importation. Article 13 imposes a due-diligence duty on economic operators and deems it satisfied merely by checking the list. The decree's own title is "Medidas relativas a la prohibicion del trabajo forzoso u obligatorio" -- prohibition of forced LABOUR, not of imports. So there is no sentence anywhere barring entry, and the regime is additionally not self-executing: it keys off a "Lista Oficial de Bienes" that DOES NOT YET EXIST, whose parameters are due within 60 natural days of entry into force per the Transitorio Unico. This is an enacted, published instrument, so limb (a) (a merely tabled measure) does not apply; it is a real but incomplete regime falling short of a full import prohibition, which is Partial under LIMB (c), the same limb as the United Kingdom. Decree signed 7 September 2026 by Laura Fernandez Delgado with Hacienda, MTSS (Mercedes Flores Badilla) and COMEX (Indiana Trejos Gallo); published 28 September; Article 17 puts it in force from La Gaceta publication, so it IS in force. Expediente 19.323 remains closed and unrelated. WHAT WOULD MOVE THIS ROW TO YES: publication of the Lista Oficial together with an instrument that actually bars entry rather than triggering "seguimiento y control". OCTOBER 2, 2026: no Lista Oficial and no further instrument yet, as expected -- the 60-natural-day parameter deadline falls around late November, so nothing is due for weeks. Monumental independently confirms the central point of the reclassification, reporting that the decree "does not yet identify specific products". COMEX and MTSS sites were not fetched, so the absence of a list there is a search-level negative rather than a site-level one. OCTOBER 3, 2026 -- THAT GAP IS NOW CLOSED AT SITE LEVEL. COMEX (home, decretos-resoluciones and sala-de-prensa) and MTSS (home) were fetched directly, with ZERO hits for "forzos", "45941" or "lista oficial de bienes" on the COMEX decretos-resoluciones page or the MTSS home. SO THE ABSENCE OF A LISTA OFICIAL IS NOW A SITE-LEVEL NEGATIVE ON THE PAGES NAMED rather than merely an absence of news -- though not exhaustive, since the decree itself does not appear in the COMEX listings either. This is expected: the 60-natural-day parameter deadline falls around late November, so nothing is due for weeks. OCTOBER 4, 2026: no list published and nothing new; COMEX and MTSS were NOT fetched today, so this is search-level rather than yesterday's site-level check. Summary and Source: President Abinader issued Decreto num. 502-26 on July 23, 2026 -- the day the 12.5% US tariff took effect -- establishing an administrative procedure empowering the Direccion General de Aduanas (DGA), coordinated with the Labor Ministry, Public Ministry, Industry and Commerce and Foreign Affairs, to identify, restrict and prohibit importation of merchandise produced wholly or partly with forced labor. Summary and Source: USTR credits the EU with an enacted prohibition but assesses enforcement as inadequate because Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is not applicable until December 14, 2027. Article 3 verified directly from EUR-Lex: "Economic operators shall not place or make available on the Union market products that are made with forced labour, nor shall they export such products." The Regulation is marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," the basis for Norway's incorporation, and Article 2(1) defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29. The Commission's implementation guidelines of June 26, 2026 (C(2026) 4386 final) and the Forced Labour Single Portal are confirmed on the Commission's own initiative page, with implementation-readiness webinars scheduled from September 2026. SCHEDULE CONFIRMED this run: the Commission's programme opens in September 2026 with a general introduction to the Forced Labour Regulation and its preparedness package, followed by SME-focused guidance sessions and sector-specific sessions running through November 2026, including a dedicated TEXTILE-sector workshop on October 20, 2026. All of this is readiness support for a prohibition that still does not apply until December 14, 2027, so the classification is unaffected. NEW this run and verified directly against EUR-Lex: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026, adopted under Article 7(7)(a) of Reg. 2024/3015, specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system for the Regulation -- a dedicated forced-labour module within ICSMS (the market-surveillance system under Reg. (EU) 2019/1020), used for the general-provisions, investigations, decisions and enforcement chapters and for data exchange between the Commission, national competent authorities and customs. Its Article 11 provides that it enters into force on the twentieth day following publication in the Official Journal. THAT DATE IS NOW CONFIRMED FROM THE PRIMARY TEXT, retrieved directly from EUR-Lex this run: the implementing regulation is dated 24 April 2026 and its OJ citation is "OJ L, 2026/903, 27.4.2026," so the twentieth day following publication is 17 May 2026 -- which corroborates the date previously carried here only on secondary reporting. Its subject matter is also now stated precisely from the title: it specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system to be used for the purposes of Regulation (EU) 2024/3015. All of this is machinery for a still-inapplicable prohibition, so classification is unchanged. A NEAR-MISS WORTH RECORDING, September 12: a research pass's search synthesis initially described a "US-EU Framework Agreement of August 21, 2026" containing a forced-labour clause, which would have been a new bilateral instrument and material to this row. The pass checked it against the primary source titles before reporting it and found the Joint Statement is dated August 21, 2025 -- a year earlier, with terms effective September 1, 2025 -- and therefore predates and is superseded by the 2026 Section 301 action rather than being new. It was rejected before adoption. Logged because it is the same failure mode as the Peruvian expediente number and the Mexican March date: a plausible, specific, confidently stated fact that dissolves on contact with the source, and here the year was the only thing wrong with it. Source: EUR-Lex (primary texts of Reg. 2024/3015 and Implementing Reg. 2026/903); European Commission initiative 16292 and C(2026) 4386 final, June 26, 2026.

Summary and Source: Guatemala's Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026 (published July 6, 2026) secured it the 10% tier. Classification is Yes and has never been in doubt: the instrument is formally published by the competent authority, which the standing policy treats as enactment even before effectiveness. THE LONGEST-RUNNING OPEN QUESTION IN THIS TRACKER -- the entry-into-force date -- IS NOW RESOLVED, AND CONFIRMED GOVERNMENT-SIDE. Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026 (18:24h, Rosa Maria Bolanos), retrieved and read directly this run, reports: "El 17 de agosto del 2026 entro en vigencia el Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, que prohibe en Guatemala las importaciones de bienes producidos mediante trabajo forzoso y obligatorio." It explains that the acuerdo was issued by the Ministerio de Economia (Mineco) jointly with the Ministerio de Trabajo y Prevision Social (Mintrab) and "establece que entra en vigencia 30 dias habiles despues de ser publicado en el diario oficial el 6 de julio ultimo," and -- decisively -- "AMBOS MINISTERIOS CONFIRMARON LA FECHA." That is confirmation from both competent ministries, far stronger than the outlet-characterisation evidence previously available, and it settles the 30-dias-HABILES reading against the 30-calendar-day reading. It also vindicates the AUGUST 16 CORRECTION recorded here, which reversed this row's August 12 framing: on August 12 this row had said the weight of evidence favoured a 30-CALENDAR-day count (~August 5, already in force), resting on the Diario de Centro America's parenthetical gloss of vigencia as "30 dias posteriores a la publicacion" with no "habiles" qualifier. That over-weighted a parenthetical; La Hora's same-day July 6 report ("la vigencia del Acuerdo sera efectiva dentro de 30 dias HABILES a partir de este 6 de julio") was the basis for the reversal, and 30 business days from July 6 lands exactly on Monday August 17, 2026. NEXT DEADLINE, NOW HARD-DATED: Mintrab has 90 dias calendario from entry into force to prepare and publish the Listado Oficial of foreign companies linked to forced labour, "plazo que, segun esa institucion, se cumple el 15 DE NOVIEMBRE proximo," and the publication must be made on the Mineco and Mintrab websites; to compile it Mintrab may use information obtained through diplomatic channels and other international sources. Economy Minister Gabriela Garcia said on Tuesday August 18 that Mintrab has asked the Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores (Minex) to request the list of companies through diplomatic channels. Article 4 of the acuerdo carries the prohibition itself: "Se prohibe la importacion de bienes extranjeros extraidos, producidos o manufacturados total o parcialmente mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio." NEW THIS RUN, retrieved and read directly: a further Prensa Libre report ("Importaciones en Guatemala: expertos advierten riesgos por acuerdo sobre trabajo forzoso") sets out the implementation mechanics and the criticism of them. Mintrab is to compile the Listado Oficial by requesting information "por conducto diplomatico," updating it annually or when circumstances change, and MINECO is the body that transmits the list to the customs authority for the corresponding controls -- so SAT acts only once it receives the list, and no SAT implementing circular has been published. Ruben Morales, a former Economy Minister and foreign-trade specialist, and the other experts interviewed say the acuerdo's provisions are very broad, that it sets out no methodology for identifying goods linked to forced labour and provides for no independent Guatemalan investigation, leaving it dependent on foreign lists, and that it requires coordination between Mineco, Mintrab and SAT that is not clearly specified. These are implementation risks, not classification questions: the instrument is enacted and in force. Source: Prensa Libre, August 18 and August 2026; La Hora, July 6, 2026; Diario de Centro America (official gazette outlet), July 2026.

RTA-SEARCH RESULT WORTH RECORDING, August 15, 2026: a new US-Guyana bilateral instrument signed on August 11, 2026 was checked because the standing methodology requires following up any US bilateral deal regardless of headline framing. It is a defence/security arrangement -- a Guyana Defence Force / State Department liaison-officer memorandum -- not a trade agreement, and it carries no forced-labour or import-prohibition clause. It therefore does NOT place Guyana on the RTA-commitment watchlist. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Guyana, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.

Summary and Source: Honduras testified at the July 7 USTR hearing (Melvin Redondo, Presidential Office of Foreign Trade), announcing an executive decree creating an express prohibition on importing forced-labour-made goods, and requested a 10% "bridge rate." The Council of Ministers approved the decree on the night of July 16, 2026; it was published the next day as Decreto Ejecutivo No. PCM-014-2026 in La Gaceta No. 37,196 (July 17, 2026), citing ILO Conventions 29/105 and CAFTA-DR obligations. Article 4 prohibits importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced/compulsory labour, effective on publication, and Article 7 directs Customs to build the prohibited-goods list into its risk-management system, with intercepted goods facing re-export or destruction at importer cost. THE IMPLEMENTING LIST HAS NOW BEEN PUBLISHED, AND THIS ROW CORRECTS A SUSTAINED ERROR OF ITS OWN. Acuerdo Ministerial No. SETRASS-527-2026 -- "Regulacion para la implementacion del Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026 y aprobacion de la Lista de Mercancias con Prohibicion de Importacion, Primera Edicion 2026" -- was published as item 1 of La Gaceta Edition No. 37,226 of AUGUST 21, 2026, signed by Labour Secretary Fernando Puerto Castro. I read the full text directly. Article 32 puts the Acuerdo in force on the day of publication; Article 28 approves the Annex I list "integrada por seis registros"; and Article 29 defers the prohibition itself, so it "empezara a implementarse treinta dias calendario despues de la publicacion" -- i.e. ENFORCEMENT BEGINS SEPTEMBER 20, 2026. HOW THE LIST WAS BUILT, which is the substantively interesting part: the Permanent Technical Commission reported on August 14 that ILO, UN Special Rapporteur, Walk Free and US Department of Labor reports establish forced-labour practices in given countries or sectors but do NOT identify a specific producer or supply chain, so listing countries or regions from them would assume all their goods are tainted and create discrimination and trade barriers contrary to Article 6 of the decree. The Commission therefore built the First Edition EXCLUSIVELY from homologated US CBP Final Determinations (Findings), expressly excluding Withhold Release Orders as resting only on reasonable suspicion. It also declined to adopt the Xinjiang (UFLPA) entity list, reasoning that it was issued by an authority other than the customs authority and so is not shown to be equivalent under Article 3(e) -- left open for later editions. Article 14 forbids listings by tariff chapter, sector, country or region without an identified producer, and goods from prison establishments require extra analysis against the ILO C29 Article 2(2)(c) penal-labour exception. The six Annex I registros are five Chinese producers plus one fishing vessel: the Da Wang (operated by Yong Feng Fishery Ltd, Vanuatu-Taiwan, 87 FR 4634); Inner Mongolia Hengzheng Group Baoanzhao Agriculture, Industry and Trade (stevia extracts, 85 FR 66574); Tianjin Malleable Iron Factory a.k.a. Tianjin No. 2 prison (malleable iron pipe fittings, 61 FR 17956); Qinghai Hide & Garment Factory (sheepskins and leather); and two further Chinese producers. HS references are indicative only until Honduran Customs fixes the exact CAI classification under Article 15. The Honduran Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCIT) has been warning importers that non-compliance could see goods blocked at the border. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026; La Gaceta No. 37,196 of July 17, 2026 and No. 37,226 of August 21, 2026, both read directly via leyes.hn; Hondudiario and Proceso Digital, August 2026. USTR's final determination of July 23, 2026 confirmed a 10% tariff for Honduras.

USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% (net of MFN) for Japan, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. OPEN QUESTION RAISED THIS RUN, from the primary text and NOT acted on: the companion Presidential Document (Federal Register doc 2026-15274), which I retrieved and read directly, states that "for goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements and would be appropriate to encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor imports." That sentence groups this economy with Taiwan, whose Partial classification rests precisely on an RTA forced-labour commitment, and its phrase "commitments regarding forced labor imports" could be read as implying one exists here too. It is NOT being treated as establishing one: the sentence is about how the tariff is calculated (netting against MFN) and about encouragement, the tariff outcome here is the 12.5% top-up rather than the 10% tier given to commitment economies, and no agreement text containing a forced-labour import-prohibition clause has been located. SETTLED THIS RUN, AND THE ANSWER IS NO. The only US-Japan instrument in force is the 2025 framework agreement announced July 22, 2025 and implemented by Executive Order 14345 of September 4, 2025 with Federal Register notices 2025-17389 and 2025-17908. Its substantive terms cover a 15% baseline tariff, sectoral carve-outs for autos, aerospace, pharmaceuticals and natural resources, Japanese purchase commitments on agricultural goods, energy and aircraft, an investment facility, and recognition of US auto standards -- and contain NO forced-labour, Section 307 or import-prohibition clause. No separate 2026 US-Japan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade exists, and Japan does not appear among the economies whose ARTs carry forced-labour commitments. The Presidential Document's "commitments regarding forced labor imports" phrasing is therefore encouraging or aspirational language in Japan's case, not a reference to an existing treaty clause. Japan stays No, and this question should not be reopened without new evidence of an actual instrument. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026; Federal Register doc 2026-15274 (primary text).

Flagged for the tracker but OUTSIDE its scope: Ebrard has warned of a separate pending Section 301 "excess manufacturing capacity" investigation covering 16 economies that could bring fresh tariffs as early as August 2026 -- unrelated to forced labor and not tracked here. OCTOBER 4, 2026 -- MEXICO IS A SIGNATORY TO THE G20 MILWAUKEE STATEMENT OF 2 OCTOBER 2026 -- the run's one genuinely new cross-cutting development, read here in full from the primary PDF on ustr.gov (2 pages, 3,657 characters). Its signatories are EXACTLY THREE: "We, the Trade Ministers of the United States, Argentina, and Mexico". Its operative passage is: "we recognize our opportunity and responsibility to work together to eliminate goods produced with forced labor from supply chains and international trade, including by adopting or maintaining and effectively enforcing measures that prohibit the importation or sale of goods produced wholly or in part with forced labor", together with "We support the exchange of information on traded goods produced with forced labor and best practices... including forced labor import prohibitions or market bans." IT CREATES NO NEW OBLIGATION AND CHANGES NO CLASSIFICATION, and the reasons are textual rather than assumed: it is a ministerial STATEMENT, not a treaty; its verbs are hortatory ("We call on all countries", "We encourage World Trade Organization Members"); and the key phrase is "adopting OR MAINTAINING", which is satisfied by what a signatory already has. It is therefore NOT an RTA commitment and does not add anyone to that watchlist. It usefully corroborates this tracker's own framing, noting that "Numerous economies have adopted, or committed to adopt, measures intended to stop the importation or placement on their market of products produced with forced labor". THE NOTABLE FACT IS THE NON-SIGNATURE OF THE OTHER SEVENTEEN G20 MEMBERS. For THIS row it is cumulative only: Mexico is already Yes on an enacted instrument, and the statement's "adopting or maintaining" language is satisfied by what it already has. Worth recording nonetheless, because Mexico is one of only three signatories alongside the US and Argentina. OCTOBER 5, 2026 -- THE LAST UNDATED MEXICAN LEAD IS DATED AND CLOSED. NZ has no forced-labour import prohibition: only a narrow prison-labour import ban under section 96 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018, which provides a pathway for a broader ban that has never been exercised. The Modern Slavery Bill is a disclosure regime rather than an import ban and remains with the Education and Workforce Select Committee, due to report back August 31, 2026 -- re-checked on August 31, 2026, the deadline day itself, with no early report-back, no extension and no import-focused amendment found -- but with the important qualification that every official route was unreachable that day (parliament.nz behind a captcha, legislation.govt.nz returning an empty 202), so the day's status rests on the absence of secondary reporting rather than on a source actually read. OPEN QUESTION RAISED THIS RUN, from the primary text and NOT acted on: the companion Presidential Document (Federal Register doc 2026-15274), which I retrieved and read directly, states that "for goods of the European Union, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, or Taiwan, section 301 tariffs that are the net of Most-Favored Nation (MFN) tariffs would be consistent with their respective Agreements on Reciprocal Trade or similar arrangements and would be appropriate to encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor imports." That sentence groups this economy with Taiwan, whose Partial classification rests precisely on an RTA forced-labour commitment, and its phrase "commitments regarding forced labor imports" could be read as implying one exists here too. It is NOT being treated as establishing one: the sentence is about how the tariff is calculated (netting against MFN) and about encouragement, the tariff outcome here is the 12.5% top-up rather than the 10% tier given to commitment economies, and no agreement text containing a forced-labour import-prohibition clause has been located. SETTLED THIS RUN, AND THE ANSWER IS NO. No KORUS FTA or Agreement on Reciprocal Trade text containing a Section 307-style IMPORT-prohibition commitment could be located. The KORUS labour chapter carries general ILO-style commitments to eliminate forced labour within Korea's own territory, which is a different thing entirely and does not qualify under the standing policy, since that requires a commitment targeting IMPORTS. Summary and Source: Taiwan's 10%-tier eligibility rests on its February 12, 2026 US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, under which Taiwan committed to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports. INSTRUMENT NOW ISSUED: on July 30, 2026 the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Ministry of Labor jointly issued the "Operating Guidelines for Restricting the Import of Forced Labor Goods" and a companion "Review Committee Establishment Guidelines," under Article 11 of the Foreign Trade Act -- the administrative instrument previously recorded here as forthcoming. A 12-member review committee co-chaired by the MOEA and MOL ministers must decide within 30 days of receiving a forced-labour referral, after which the competent authority publishes a notice restricting or lifting the import restriction, with Customs and the Finance Ministry notifying importers to return or destroy listed goods. Column 6 accordingly upgraded to Taiwan's own Ministry of Labor announcement. Classification remains Partial on the same reasoning applied to the Philippines' Joint Administrative Order: this is an enforcement regime under existing statutory authority, not a standalone enacted import prohibition, and no Legislative Yuan bill has been tabled (the separate Employment Service Act amendments address labour brokerage, not imports). SEQUENCE CLARIFIED this run: the Executive Yuan approved the mechanism on July 29, 2026 and MOEA/MOL formally announced it the following day, July 30 -- the date this row already carried. Also new: Amnesty International Taiwan is publicly pressing the government to LEGISLATE the labour provisions of the US-Taiwan agreement rather than continue relying on administrative guidelines, which is the step that would move Taiwan from Partial to Yes; no Legislative Yuan bill has been tabled. Source: Public Television Service (PTS) and Executive Yuan Section 301 portal, July 29-30, 2026; Amnesty International Taiwan; Ministry of Labor (Taiwan, official), July 30, 2026; Newtalk and Taipei Times, July 30-31, 2026; USTR fact sheet, February 2026.

Summary and Source: Thailand's Cabinet (June 23, 2026) approved the "Committee on Determining Standards for Imported Goods at Risk of Forced Labour or Services," chaired by the Labour Minister, to set Watchlist/Blacklist/Risk List criteria under Section 5 of the Export and Import of Goods Act B.E. 2522 (1979); re-checked August 13, 2026 against the Royal Gazette (ratchakitcha.soc.go.th) and Thai-language sources, no proclamation, watchlist or blacklist has been published. NEW this run, and it does NOT change the classification: Thai reporting indicates the Labour Ministry is DRAFTING a bill for eventual submission to parliament, and Commerce Minister Suphajee has said the US undervalues Thailand's efforts. Re-confirmed August 14 via Thai-language reporting (Prachatai, Kaohoon, Nation Thailand, prd.go.th) that the bill remains at the DRAFTING stage and has not been submitted to parliament. FURTHER NEW THIS RUN, also not enough to move the classification: the Prime Minister has directed six ministries, led by the Labour Ministry, to prepare enforcement and traceability measures. That is an executive directive to prepare, not an enacted or tabled instrument, so it stays on the No side of the line. A measure being drafted is not a measure formally tabled or published, so it falls short of the Partial threshold; if the bill is actually tabled, Thailand moves to Partial. NEW THIS RUN: the Cabinet-established Committee on Determining Standards for Imported Goods at Risk of Forced Labour or Services held its FIRST meeting on August 14, 2026, per the Ministry of Labour's own announcement (mol.go.th), agreeing to establish subcommittees and to draft screening standards and guidelines. That is the committee beginning to organise itself, not an instrument: no Royal Gazette proclamation, watchlist or blacklist has issued from it, so Thailand stays No. It does show the Section 5 route is live rather than dormant, and it is the first concrete activity from this committee since its June 23 creation. Thailand held technical talks with USTR in May. Source: Mahanakorn Partners Group / Bloomberg Tax, June 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Thailand, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (committee established under existing trade law; no Royal Gazette proclamation, watchlist or blacklist published as of August 21, 2026, though the committee held its first meeting on August 14, 2026 and agreed to form subcommittees and draft screening standards; the Labour Ministry's bill is still only being drafted, not tabled, and a new PM directive to six ministries to prepare enforcement measures remains at the directive stage. Routing clarified September 1, 2026: the Cabinet decision is being channelled to the Department of Foreign Trade to issue a Royal Gazette notice under Section 5 of the Export and Import Act -- that notice, if it appears, is the specific instrument that would move this row, and it has not appeared. RECLASSIFICATION TO PARTIAL PROPOSED THIS RUN, CONSIDERED SERIOUSLY, AND REJECTED ON THE PRIMARY TEXT. A research pass argued the June 2026 Cabinet decision satisfies the standing policy's Partial limb (iv), "a formal government decision with instrument pending." That is a fair question, so I read the Thai government's own account -- the Public Relations Department release -- rather than the secondary summaries. It says the Cabinet "มีมติเห็นชอบตามที่กระทรวงแรงงานเสนอ ในการกำหนดหลักเกณฑ์สินค้านำเข้าที่มีความเสี่ยงการใช้แรงงานบังคับ" and approved TWO things: acknowledging the investigation findings, and approving the ESTABLISHMENT of a "คณะกรรมการกำหนดมาตรฐานสินค้านำเข้าที่มีความเสี่ยงจากการบังคับใช้แรงงานหรือบริการ" chaired by the Labour Minister. That committee's function is to set criteria and document-verification standards and to PROPOSE a Watchlist/Blacklist/Risk List back TO THE CABINET ("เสนอบัญชีรายชื่อเสี่ยง ... ต่อ ครม.").
